title: Yearning for the Land of Ultimate Bliss, Wearying of the Sahā World
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The sufferings of the Sahā world are beyond all words; the bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss lies beyond all description.

inline.s: The sufferings of the Sahā world are beyond all words; the bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss lies beyond all description.

Faith, vow, and practice are the three provisions of the Pure Land path. Of these, the vow means to yearn for the Land of Ultimate Bliss and to weary of the Sahā world. Therefore, while a Buddha-recitation practitioner advances in recitation, he should also cultivate the practice of yearning and wearying, and put it into practice in daily life. This is the concrete expression of faith and vow.

blocks.text: Yearning for the Land of Ultimate Bliss

inline.s: Why yearn for the Land of Ultimate Bliss? Because the living beings of that land are free from all suffering and experience only every bliss, and what is more, this is the golden path that fulfills the bodhi vow of universally saving living beings and together accomplishing the Buddha way!
In the Amitabha Sūtra, the Buddha says:

Śāriputra, why is that land called the Land of Ultimate Bliss? The living beings of that land are free from all suffering and experience only every bliss; therefore it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Among all the sufferings there are the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, the ten sufferings, and the one hundred and ten sufferings, and moreover the suffering of the two kinds of birth-and-death (birth-and-death of delimited portions and birth-and-death of transformation).

The three sufferings are the suffering of suffering, the suffering of decay, and the suffering of conditioning. First, the suffering of suffering: worldly beings already have a body subject to birth and death, which is suffering enough; when further pressed and scorched by yet more sorrows, it becomes suffering piled upon suffering—hence the suffering of suffering. Second, the suffering of decay: the pleasure that appears only briefly, and the suffering felt the moment it is lost. Third, the suffering of conditioning: all conditioned things are impermanent, flowing on without ceasing, never at rest.

The eight sufferings: first, the suffering of birth—the pain of being born; second, the suffering of aging—the pain of the weakening body; third, the suffering of illness—the pain of sickness; fourth, the suffering of death—the pain at the time of dying; fifth, the suffering of separation from what one loves; sixth, the suffering of meeting with what one hates; seventh, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; eighth, the suffering of the raging five skandhas—because of the illusory body and mind produced by the five skandhas (form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness), one gives rise to delusion on contact with the six sense objects and creates karma, subjected to torment that blazes like fire and cannot be stilled.

[Five Yin] An old translation of the five skandhas. Yin means to cover and obstruct—these five cover the true thusness of Dharma-nature and give rise to all afflictions. [The Five Skandhas] The skandhas of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. These five arise through accumulation, and so are called the skandhas; they can also cover a person's true nature, causing delusion and topsy-turvy, and creating all karma—hence they are also called the five yin. Of these, form refers to matter and is called the dharma of form; the four skandhas of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness belong to the mind and are called the dharmas of mind. These are the five great elements that constitute body and mind, of which form is the body and the other four are the mind.
Regarding the ten sufferings and the one hundred and ten sufferings, Master Lianchi, in his Commentary and Sub-Commentary on the Amitabha Sūtra, says:

“The ten sufferings, as the Bodhisattva Treasury Sutra sets out: first, the suffering of birth; second, the suffering of old age; and so on, up to the tenth, the suffering of the flow of birth and death. As for the one hundred and ten sufferings, the Treatise on the Stages of Yoga Practice sets them out: first, the undifferentiated suffering of the flow [of transmigration]; second, the suffering of desire; third, the suffering of delusion; up to the fifty-fifth suffering; then nine further kinds of suffering, and within those nine, each in turn is opened out into fifty-five, so that together they make one hundred and ten sufferings.”

None of these sufferings exist at all in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. As for the suffering of the two kinds of birth-and-death, one who is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is born by transformation from within a lotus, so there is no delimited birth-and-death, and he attains the stage of non-retrogression. How then could the suffering of transformative birth-and-death be a concern? Hence it is said to be free from all suffering.

[The Two Kinds of Birth-and-Death] Delimited birth-and-death and transformative birth-and-death. [Delimited Birth-and-Death] For beings within the three realms and six paths, because of the karma of good and evil deeds, their lifespans all have limits and their bodies all have distinct forms, so their birth and death are called delimited birth-and-death. One who has ended delimited birth-and-death escapes the wheel of transmigration and leaves the three realms. [Transformative Birth-and-Death] For the sages of the three vehicles, having cut off the delusions of views and thought and ended delimited birth-and-death, in the course of their practice deluded thoughts gradually cease while realization gradually increases. This movement from delusion to awakening differs in each period, and the transition from an earlier stage to a later one is like a single birth-and-death; such transformations are wondrous, unfathomable, and inconceivable—hence it is called transformative birth-and-death. One who has ended transformative birth-and-death perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
The Amitabha Sūtra
says:
“Experience only every bliss.”
As for every bliss, the Cloud-of-Compassion Penitent, contrasting the suffering of this world with the bliss of that land, enumerated ten kinds:

First: in this world there is the suffering of seldom meeting the Buddha, while in that land there is no such suffering, but only the joy of seeing the Buddha when the lotus opens and being able to draw near him. Second: in this world there is the suffering of not hearing the Dharma preached, while in that land there is no such suffering, but only the joy of water, birds, trees, and groves all proclaiming the wondrous Dharma. Third: the suffering of being entangled by evil companions, versus the joy of being gathered with all the wise and virtuous in a single assembly. Fourth: the suffering of being disturbed by a host of demons, versus the joy of being kept in mind and guarded by all the Buddhas, far removed from all demonic matters. Fifth: the suffering of endless rebirth, versus the joy of cutting across birth and death and forever escaping the wheel. Sixth: the suffering of the unavoidable three evil paths, versus the joy of having left the evil realms so far that their very names are no longer heard. Seventh: the suffering of worldly conditions blocking the path, versus the joy of natural enjoyment that requires no striving. Eighth: the suffering of a short span of life, versus the joy of a lifespan equal to the Buddha, beyond all limit. Ninth: the suffering of regressing in practice, versus the joy of entering the stage of right samādhi with no turning back. Tenth: the suffering of barely succeeding after aeons of kalpas, versus the joy of a single lifetime completing the practice and accomplishing all that is to be done.

[Rightly-joined Group] One of the three groups. [The Three Groups] The three groups are three classes of beings, namely the rightly joined group, the wrongly joined group, and the not-yet-fixed group. The rightly joined group refers to the class of beings who are certain to realize the Way; the wrongly joined group refers to the class of beings who can never realize it; the not-yet-fixed group refers to those between right and wrong, who may realize the Way or may not realize it.
[Aeon of Dust] That is

the kalpa of three-thousand dust-motes: grind everything within a great chiliocosm into ink; every time one passes through a great chiliocosm, deposit a single mote; when the ink is used up, and all the worlds passed through have crumbled into dust, then take each mote of dust as one kalpa to count the number of kalpas. This is a metaphor expressing a span of time of inconceivable length.
The Jewel Mirror of the Pure Land School says:

“In the defiled region of the Sahā world, all the sufferings gather and the quest for the Way is hard to accomplish; in the joyful land of the Pure Land, all the virtues cluster and one ascends to a stage of non-retrogression. Those who call upon the name are kept in mind by the Buddhas and are reborn there; those who arouse the bodhi-mind are illumined by Amitabha and advance. Bodhisattvas and arhats become their fellows,
(their companions),

and water, birds, trees, and groves all recite the Buddha. The ear ever hears the wondrous Dharma; in the heart greed and anger suddenly cease. Joy is without limit, how boundless the span of life! Born in that land, one at once attains avaivartika—
(Skt. avaivartika, also translated avivartika, meaning non-retrogression toward Buddhahood; this is an important stage in the bodhisattva's practice)

,—how could this compare to the paths of humans and gods, where the eye meets much that thwarts and much that favors? On the way of the provisional vehicles, wholesome roots are rarely brought to fulfillment; the three worthies before the ground have not yet seen the Way and lose mindfulness. ...From this we know that if the practitioners of the three vehicles pass through kalpas
(asaṃkhyeya kalpas)

their meritorious practice gains no accomplishment, while through the gate of Buddha-recitation in a snap of the fingers one attains a stage of non-retrogression. Thus those born in the Pure Land, being only good and never evil, never retreat and are certain to become Buddhas. Therefore the Amitabha Sūtra says: the living beings born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss all are avivartika. Alas! The first-mind of the beginner holds shallow faith; without the power of another it is hard to advance. Our Buddha's vow is deep; all who have affinity are gathered in. Only believe: in other gates the study of the Way is like an ant's
(an ant)

climbing a high mountain, whereas birth in the Pure Land is like a sailboat running before a fair wind. Amitabha, by his welcoming, leads straight to bodhi; the assembly of sages, by their supporting, lifts one beyond the three realms. The upper grade ascends at once to the fruit of Buddhahood; even the lower birth surpasses the celestial palaces. Believe all of this and doubt not; together practice with non-retrogression.”

[Provisional Vehicle] The bodhisattvas of the provisional vehicle refer to the bodhisattvas of the three teachings—the store, the shared, and the distinct. Because their meritorious practice is still shallow, they have not actually reached the true bodhisattva stage. [The Three Worthies] In the process of Mahāyāna practice, among the fifty-two stages from ordinary being to sage, the bodhisattvas of the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten dedications, having cut off only the delusions of views and thought and still possessing the dust-like delusions and delusions of fundamental ignorance, have not yet entered the sage stages of the ten grounds; therefore they are called the three worthies, or the bodhisattvas before the ground.
Master Yinguang instructed:
“The sufferings of the Sahā world are beyond words; the bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss lies beyond all description.”

He then drew a vivid contrast between these two worlds, pointing out that one should make earnest vows, vowing to leave the suffering of the Sahā world and to attain the bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. His words read:

“The sufferings of the Sahā world are without measure or limit. In sum, they do not go beyond the eight sufferings, namely birth, aging, sickness, death, separation from the beloved, meeting the hateful, not obtaining what is sought, and the raging of the five skandhas. These eight sufferings—from the most exalted of an age down to the lowliest beggar—every person has them all. The first seven are fruits reaped in past lives; think on them deeply and you will know them yourself, nor need they be spoken of at length, for to do so would consume too much ink and words. The eighth, the suffering of the raging five skandhas, is the rising of thought and the stirring of mind in the present, and is the seed of suffering to come. Cause and fruit are linked and continue without break, from kalpa to kalpa without release. The five skandhas are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Form is the body that is the karmic reward; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the deluded mind that arises upon contact with objects. Through this deluded body and mind and these dharmas, in the presence of the six sense objects one gives rise to delusion and creates karma, blazing like fire and unable to be stilled—hence it is called raging. Moreover, yin means to cover and conceal; its sound and meaning are the same as shade. Through these five dharmas the true nature is covered and cannot be made manifest. Just as thick clouds veil the sun—though the radiance of that brilliant
(gǎo, meaning bright)
sun is in no way diminished, yet because of the clouds it is not illumined by it—so too, ordinary beings who have not cut off delusion and karma, being obstructed by these five dharmas
(form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness),

it is the same: the sun of wisdom in the sky of one's nature cannot be made manifest. This eighth suffering is the root of all the other sufferings. The cultivator of the Way, whose power of meditation is deep, has no clinging at all toward the six sense objects and gives rise neither to aversion nor to attachment. Advancing further, applying the practice with diligent effort, he attains realization of non-arising; then delusion and karma are completely cleansed and the root of birth and death is severed. Yet this accomplishment is far from easy; in the last age, those who attain it are truly few. Hence one must single-mindedly cultivate the pure karma and seek birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, relying on the Buddha's compassionate power to be reborn in the West. Having attained rebirth there, one is born by transformation within a lotus and has no suffering of birth. In the pure form of a true youth, with a lifespan equal to empty space, the body is free of calamity, change, aging, sickness, and death; their very names are not heard, let alone their reality. Following the assembly of sages and personally serving Amitabha, water, birds, trees, and groves all give forth the sounds of the Dharma; according to one's own faculties, through hearing one realizes. One's very kin are nowhere to be found, how much less an enemy! Think of clothing and clothing comes; think of food and food comes; towers, pavilions, halls, and dwellings are all formed of the seven jewels, without the aid of human effort, purely transformed into being. Then the seven sufferings of the Sahā world are overturned to become seven blisses. As for the body, it has great supernormal powers and great might; without leaving the very spot, in a single thought it can, throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, accomplish all the Buddha-deeds, seeking the highest above and transforming beings below. As for the mind, it has great wisdom and great eloquence; within a single dharma it fully knows the true characteristics of all dharmas and speaks the Dharma in accord with beings' capacities without error. Though it speaks in conventional terms, all accord with the wondrous principle of true reality. It does not suffer the raging of the five skandhas but enjoys the bliss of body and mind in quiescence and cessation. Therefore the Sutra says: free from all suffering, experiencing only every bliss, hence called the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once one knows the Sahā world to be suffering and the Land of Ultimate Bliss to be bliss, one should make earnest vows, vowing to leave the suffering of the Sahā world and to attain the bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The urgency of this vow should be like one who has fallen into a latrine-pit, anxious to get out, and like one bound in prison, eagerly thinking of home.”
(from the Recorded Sayings of Master Yinguang)
In the Qing
(the Qing dynasty),
Master Daoche, a man of Qiantang. After leaving the home life and questing under a teacher, he awakened to what was originally his own
(saw his nature).
He then single-mindedly cultivated the pure karma. Dwelling at the Manjushri Hermitage in Hangzhou, he set a term
(an allotted period)
for a closed-door retreat, keeping nothing superfluous in the room
(nothing extra in the retreat room)
,—only a small table and a single low couch
(only a small table and a bed).
Within only a few days he was taken gravely ill
(only a few days after entering the retreat
he fell ill, growing ever more severe),
so he roused himself
(nerving himself)
and said: The practice of Buddha-recitation is precisely for the matter of birth and death
(the closed retreat's recitation is precisely to end birth and death);
how can it be cut short for the sake of illness
chuò
, to give up)
? How can one abandon the retreat and seek a physician because of illness?
(How could he give up the retreat for medical care because of illness?)
Then he held the Buddha's name all the more earnestly. Soon
(before long)
a golden light filled the room, the Buddha placed his hand upon his head, and the illness was instantly cured.

Thereupon he attained the samādhi of Buddha-recitation; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he had no different thought at all. After three years in this way, on the fifteenth day of the third month
(the fifteenth day of the third lunar month)
he came out of retreat. When he had ascended the seat and finished preaching the Dharma, he said to the assembly: I shall pass to the West after the fifteenth of the seventh month
(the fifteenth day of the seventh month);
you may all come to see me off. When the time arrived
(when the fifteenth of the seventh month came),
as he was
(just)
holding the Ullambana assembly, and the multitude gathered
(the people gathered together),
recalling his earlier words
(someone brought up the master's earlier words that he would pass away after the fifteenth of the seventh month),
the master said: It is so;
(such a thing there is),
wait a little. The next day he handed over the abbotship, set out a meal to take leave of the assembly, entered the shrine, sat with closed eyes, and ceased to breathe. After a moment he revived
(he came to again shortly),
and said: In taking this long leave of you all, how can I be without a word?
The sufferings of the Sahā world cannot be told; the bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss cannot be told.

If you would keep me in mind, simply recite Amitabha Buddha, and before long we shall meet. Should you miss this life, you will turn in the long night [of transmigration]—how painful! how painful! Having spoken, he passed away, aged forty-eight.
(from the Record of Pure Land Worthies)

[Ullambana Assembly] Ullambana is translated as releasing those hung upside down. After death a person may fall into the three evil paths, where they suffer intensely, as if suspended upside down. Basin (bana) is a vessel for containing food. Ullambana means: using a basin to hold all kinds of precious and delicious foods to offer to the Buddhas and the monastic community, so that, relying on the inconceivable field of merit of the Three Jewels, one may deliver one's departed ancestors from the suffering of hanging upside down. The Ullambana Assembly is therefore the Dharma-assembly held each year on the fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month, when various offerings are generously set out and presented to the Three Jewels to relieve the departed ancestors of the suffering of hanging upside down.
Master Yinguang said:
“When a Buddha-recitation practitioner is ill, he should single-mindedly await death. If the allotted span of this life is not yet exhausted, he will instead recover all the more quickly, for
(because)
reciting the Buddha with the whole body freely let go most effectively erases karma; when karma is erased the illness is cured. If one does not let go but seeks to be healed
(seeks to be cured),
then should he fail to recover, he will certainly have no way to be reborn there, for he did not wish to be born
(because he did not wish to seek rebirth);

if one does not understand this principle, how can he still obtain the support of the Buddha's compassionate power? In your mother's illness you should earnestly urge her to let go and seek rebirth; if her lifespan is not exhausted, seeking rebirth will instead hasten her recovery, for through the utmost sincerity of mind she obtains the compassionate protection of the Buddha.”
(from the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang: A Letter in Reply to the Brothers Zhou Mengyou)
Master Shandao said:

“Whoever, at the end of life, wishes to be reborn in the Pure Land must not be afraid to die. Ever mindful that this body is full of suffering and entangled with all manner of impure defilements and evil karma, if one can cast off this defiled body and transcend to birth in the Pure Land, receiving immeasurable joy and being released from the suffering states of birth and death, that is truly a satisfying matter: like taking off shabby clothes and exchanging them for precious robes. One should simply let go of body and mind and give rise to no clinging. Whenever illness comes, contemplate impermanence and with a single mind await death.”
(from Venerable Shandao's Essay on Right Mindfulness at the Moment of Death for Rebirth)

[Impermanence] All dharmas in the world arise and cease, flowing on without resting even for an instant; this is called impermanence. Impermanence is a hallmark of this Sahā world. For living beings with life and breath (humans among them), there is birth, aging, sickness, and death. For inanimate things—minerals, tools, and even mountains, rivers, and the great earth—there are formation, abiding, decay, and emptiness. To know impermanence thoroughly is to understand that whatever arises must cease, whatever gathers must scatter, whatever rises must fall; all things pass, and in the blink of an eye all is empty. Ending birth and death is then the matter of first importance, and one will not give rise to greed for pleasing things and situations nor hatred for disagreeable ones—and greed and hatred are the very root of the wheel of birth and death. At the same time, to know impermanence thoroughly is to be constantly warned: life is short and the world is fragile; one must seize the time to cultivate, for when a single breath is gone one belongs to the next life.
Things passing the eye we rank as foul or fair; / When all is done, no matter is our care.

Among the three provisions of the Pure Land path—faith, vow, and practice—the vow means wearying of the Sahā world and yearning for the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore a Buddha-recitation practitioner should not only yearn for the Land of Ultimate Bliss, but should also weary of the Sahā world; this is of the utmost importance. The tenth patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Xingce, said:
“Possessing the true vow, give rise to a yearning
(xīn, the same as yearning)

and wearied heart, seeing the three realms as a prison, seeing home and family as fetters, seeing sound and beauty as deadly poison, seeing fame and profit as reins and chains, seeing the ups and downs of success and failure over the decades as a last night's dream, seeing this single life's karmic reward in the Sahā world as rest at a wayside inn, and being glad to leave the lodging, the mind fixed solely on reciting the Buddha, wishing to be born together in the Pure Land.”

“The recitation of the Buddha that keeps one's merit not in vain: rouse body and mind diligently, cherishing every inch of time; and since life hangs upon a breath, how can it last? Like a prisoner being led to the execution ground, each step draws nearer to death.
One must, with unremitting diligence,
(diligently, without ceasing),
through day and night, and painstakingly
kū kū
, toiling without rest),
through summer heat and winter cold,
so that the single great name is never interrupted even for a moment; then birth in the Pure Land is certain. Take care not to begin with vigor and end in sloth.”
(from the Essence of Master Xingce's Warnings)
Venerable Master Guangqin said:

“If emotional clinging is not broken, though the mouth recite the Buddha, thought after thought still falls back into the Sahā world. If one is earnest and sincere, letting go of all conditions, then in a single thought one can reach the West. Dragged by myriad conditions and unable to cut them away, then for a hundred years or ten thousand years one remains within the three realms.”
Then, amid the tangle of myriad conditions, how is one to accomplish the wearying of the Sahā world? Here I transcribe and annotate the relevant instructions of the patriarchs.

blocks.text: 1. The Root of Birth and Death

inline.s: In Master Hanshan's Collection from Dream-Voyaging
, the
chapter The Essential Points of Buddha-Recitation says:

[The gate of reciting the Buddha to seek birth in the Pure Land is originally for the great matter of ending birth and death. Hence it is said: reciting the Buddha ends birth and death. People today give rise to the resolve to recite the Buddha precisely because they wish to end birth and death; they only say that the Buddha can end birth and death. Yet if they do not know the root of birth and death, where in the end are they to direct their recitation? If the mind that recites the Buddha cannot cut off the root of birth and death, how can it end birth and death?]

This Dharma-gate of reciting the Buddha to seek birth in the Pure Land is originally for the great matter of ending birth and death. Hence it is said: reciting the Buddha ends birth and death. People today give rise to the resolve to recite the Buddha precisely because they wish to end birth and death; they only say that reciting the Buddha can end birth and death. Yet if they do not know the root of birth and death, where in the end are they to direct their recitation? If the mind that recites the Buddha cannot cut off the root of birth and death, how can it end birth and death?
[Root and Trunk] The root and the trunk of a plant, taken as a metaphor for the foundation of a thing.

[What is the root of birth and death? The ancients said: If karma were not heavy, one would not be born in the Sahā world; if love were not severed, one would not be born in the Pure Land. From this we know that the root of love is the root of birth and death. For all living beings who suffer the suffering of birth and death do so through the fault of love and desire. Tracing this root of love, it did not come to be only in this life, nor only in one, two, three, or four lives, but from the very beginningless beginning when birth and death first arose, life after life, giving up one body and receiving another, all has flowed on through love and desire, down to the present day. Looking back on the past, has there ever been a single thought that left this root of love even for an instant? Such seeds of the root of love, accumulated and deepened through aeons of kalpas, are why birth and death are without end.]

What then is the root of birth and death? The ancients said: If karma were not heavy, one would not be born in the Sahā world; if love were not severed, one would not be born in the Pure Land. From this we know that the root of love is the root of birth and death. For all living beings who suffer the suffering of birth and death do so through the fault of love and desire. Tracing this root of love, it was not present only in this life, nor only in one, two, three, or four lives, but from the very beginningless beginning when birth and death first arose, life after life, giving up the body (death) and receiving a body (rebirth), all has been turned by love and desire, down to the present day. Looking back on the past, has there ever been a single thought that left this root of love even for an instant? Such seeds of the root of love, accumulated and deepened through countless kalpas, are why birth and death are without limit.
[Love] The meaning of greedy attachment and defiled clinging.
The Meaning of Mahāyāna says: Greedy defilement is called love. The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says: The wheel of transmigration takes love as its root.
[Root of Love] Love gives rise to karma and its fruits, therefore it is called the root of love.
Master Sheng'an said: Reciting the Buddha is no difficult matter; the difficulty lies in a single mind. Even a single mind is no difficult matter; the difficulty lies in cutting off the root of love.

[Today one has only just resolved to recite the Buddha, hoping merely to reach the West by empty aspiration, and does not even know the very name of love as the root of birth and death—has there ever been a single thought of cutting it? Since one does not know the root of birth and death, while the recitation is being carried on on the one hand, the root of birth and death is plainly allowed to grow on the other. Such recitation has nothing whatever to do with birth and death. However you recite, when you come to the time of death you will see only the root of love in birth and death appear before you; only then will you know the Buddha has given you no strength at all, and you will blame the recitation as without effect—but the regret will be too late.]

Today one has only just resolved to recite the Buddha, hoping merely to reach the West by empty aspiration, and does not even know the fact that love is the root of birth and death—has there ever been a single thought of cutting it? Since one does not know what the root of birth and death is, while the recitation is being carried on on the one hand, the root of birth and death (love) is allowed to grow on the other. Such recitation has nothing whatever to do with escaping birth and death. Using this method, however you recite, when you come to the time of death you will see only the root of birth and death (love) appear before you; only then will you know the Buddha has given you no strength at all, and you will blame the recitation as without effect—but the regret will be too late.

[Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha today first to know that love is the root of birth and death. And, in the present recitation, thought after thought must cut off this root of love. Take daily life as it appears: reciting the Buddha while at home, the eyes see children, grandchildren, family, and property—not a single one of them but is loved—and so there is not a single matter or a single thought that is not an occupation of birth and death, like having the whole body within a pit of fire. One does not realize that even while reciting the Buddha, the root of love in the mind has not been let go for a single thought. It is just when one is actually reciting that one says only the recitation is not intense, not knowing that love is the master and recitation only the outward face. Reciting in this way, the Buddha is only chanted while love is only grown. And when the affection of children and grandchildren appears before you, turn the light back and examine: can this single sound of the Buddha truly withstand that love? Can it indeed cut off that love? If it cannot cut off this love, then how in the end are birth and death to be ended? Because the conditions of love have been familiar through many births, while the recitation of the Buddha is newly resolved and quite unfamiliar, and moreover not real and earnest, so it has no power.]

Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha today first to know that love is the root of birth and death. And, in the present recitation, thought after thought must cut off this root of love. Take the present case of reciting while at home: in daily life the eyes see children, grandchildren, family, and property—not a single one of them but is loved—and so there is not a single matter or a single thought that is not an occupation of birth and death, like having the whole body within a pit of fire. One does not realize that even while reciting the Buddha, the root of love in the mind has not been let go for a single thought. It is just when one is actually reciting that one says only the recitation is not real and earnest, not knowing the reason within—that love is the master and recitation only the outward face. Reciting in this way, the Buddha is only chanted while love is only grown. And when the affection of children and grandchildren appears before you, turn the light back and examine: can this single sound of the Buddha truly withstand that love? Can it indeed cut off that love? If it cannot cut off this love, then how in the end are birth and death to be ended? For the conditions of love have been thoroughly familiar through many births, while the recitation of the Buddha is only newly resolved and quite unfamiliar, and moreover not real and earnest, so it has no power.
[The Condition of Love] Emotional
affection and love as a condition. The Ratnakūṭa Sūtra says: Among all the afflictions, the condition of love joined together is the most weighty.

[If now one cannot be master over the realm of love before the eyes, then at the time of death one will in the end be unable to be master over it. Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha: first, know that the mind's urgency about birth and death must be keen, and the resolve to cut off birth and death must be keen, and that upon the very root of birth and death one must cut thought after thought—then every thought is the very time of ending birth and death. Why wait until the thirtieth day of the twelfth month before ending it? That would be late beyond late! As it is said: All that is before the eyes are the matters of birth and death; if now one finishes with the matters of birth and death before the eyes, birth and death are empty. If one uses the mind in this way, thought after thought genuine, every stroke drawing blood, and if with such a mind one yet fails to escape birth and death, then all the Buddhas would be speaking falsehood. Therefore, whether at home or gone forth from the home life, only to hold the mind of birth and death is the very time of escaping birth and death—how could there be any other wondrous method!]

If now one cannot be master over the realm of love before the eyes, then at the time of death one will in the end be unable to be master over it. Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha: first, realize that the mind's resolve to cut off birth and death must be keen. Having realized that the resolve to cut off birth and death must be keen, one must upon the root of birth and death (the root of love) cut thought after thought—then every thought is the very time of ending birth and death. Why wait until the thirtieth day of the twelfth month (the moment of death) before ending birth and death? If only then does one think of ending birth and death, it is late beyond late! As it is said: All that is before the eyes are the matters of birth and death; if now one finishes with the matters of birth and death before the eyes, birth and death are empty. If one uses the mind in this way, thought after thought genuine, every stroke drawing blood, and if with such a mind one yet fails to escape birth and death, then all the Buddhas would be speaking falsehood. Therefore, whether at home or gone forth from the home life, as long as one truly holds the mind of birth and death, that is the very time of escaping birth and death—how could there be any other wondrous method!

[All that is before the eyes are the matters of birth and death; if now one finishes with them, birth and death are empty] What lies before the eyes are all occupations of birth and death; to finish with these occupations of birth and death before the eyes is to finish with birth and death (to make birth and death empty).

blocks.text: 2. Severing Love and Unifying the Recitation

inline.s: [Severing Love and Unifying the Recitation] Sever one's love and unify one's mindfulness. [Severing one's love and unifying one's mindfulness] Sever the root of love and make single the mindful recitation of the Buddha.
Master Youxi, in his Dharma Words on the Pure Land, says:

[Yet to speak of it is not hard; to practice it is hard. To practice it is not hard; to grasp the essential of the mind is hard. This is the warning of people of old, and it is what we of this generation should follow. If one seeks that which is truly an earnest admonition for oneself, none is more essential than the two sayings of Yang Cigong, which are: If love were not heavy, one would not be born in the Sahā world; if mindfulness were not unified, one would not be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.]

Yet as for seeking birth in the Pure Land, to speak of it with the mouth is not hard; to practice it in reality is hard. To practice it in reality is not hard; to realize the essential of the mind in practice is hard. This is the warning of the wise ones of old, and we should earnestly heed it. If one wishes to obtain the most sincere admonition (the essential of the mind) for how one is to practice oneself, none surpasses the two sayings of Yang Cigong, which are: If love were not heavy, one would not be born in the Sahā world; if mindfulness were not unified, one would not be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[Yang Cigong] Yang Jie, styled Cigong, with the sobriquet Wuweizi. A man of the Song dynasty, he at first favored the Chan school; practicing under Chan Master Tianyi Huai, he had a great awakening. At the end of the Xining era he returned home on account of his mother's mourning (his mother's death); in retirement he read the Buddhist canon, and so turned his mind toward the Pure Land, promoting it energetically, and painted a sixteen-foot Amitabha Buddha to contemplate on his person at all times. At the moment of death he saw a golden platform come from the sky, and reciting a verse, he passed away. [If love were not heavy, one would not be born in the Sahā world] To end birth and death and escape the wheel of transmigration, one must sever love. The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says: All living beings, from beginningless time, because of manifold kinds of affection, craving, and greed, are subject to the wheel of transmigration. [If mindfulness were not unified, one would not be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss] To be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one must be single-mindedly devoted to the mindful recitation of the Buddha. This single-minded recitation is what the Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Mindfulness of the Buddha by Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta calls the pure thought continuing, and what Master Shandao calls thought following thought in continuity.

[Now, reciting the Buddha in order to unify the mind: earnestly upholding the Name, with single intent and no disorder—this is what I should devote my whole mind to. Yet sometimes one forgets and cannot recite, or recites and cannot be unified; there is no other reason than that affection and love have carried the recitation-mind away. To lighten love in order to put a stop to its delusions, to cut off the root of emotion, and to escape the net of love—this is what I should devote my whole mind to. Yet sometimes one recites but cannot forget, or forgets but cannot exhaust it; there is no other reason than that the mindful recitation-mind cannot be unified. Hence for one who recites the Buddha seeking birth in the Pure Land: if ordinarily there is a single love in the Sahā world not made light, then at death he will be drawn by that love and not be born—how much more so with many loves! And even a single thought toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss not unified will, at death, be turned by that thought and not be born—how much more so with many thoughts!]

Reciting the Buddha is in order to unify the mind. Therefore earnestly upholding the Name with single intent and no disorder is what one should devote his whole mind to. Yet sometimes one forgets and cannot recite, or recites but cannot be unified; there is no other reason than that affection and love have carried away the recitation-mind (giving rise to deluding thoughts). To lighten love in order to cut off the deluding thoughts, to sever the root of emotion, and to escape the net of love is what one should devote his whole mind to. Yet sometimes one recites but cannot forget love, or to forget love is not to forget it entirely; there is no other reason than that the recitation-mind cannot be unified. Hence for one who recites the Buddha seeking birth in the Pure Land: if in daily life there is a single love in the Sahā world not put down, then at death he will be drawn by that love and not be born—how much more so with many loves! And if there is a single thought toward seeking birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss not unified, then at death he will be turned by that un-unified thought and not be reborn—how much more so with many such un-unified thoughts!
Shěn (shěn) means how much more.

[Now, what makes love to be love includes the light and the heavy, the deep and the shallow, the main retribution and the circumstantial retribution. Enumerating its objects: father, mother, wife, and children; elder and younger brothers and friends; fame, achievement, wealth, and rank; essays, poetry, and rhapsodies; arts, techniques, and skills; clothing, drink, and food; houses, rooms, fields, and gardens; groves, springs, flowers, and plants; precious treasures and playthings—all manner of exquisite good things too many to be listed in full. The great are heavier than Mount Tai; the small are lighter than a goose's feather. To have a single thing unforgotten—that is love; to have a single thought not set aside—that is love. If there is a single love held in the heart, then the mindfulness is not unified; if there is a single thought that does not return to unity, then one will not be reborn.]
